policy_title: Close Tax Loopholes and Modernise HMRC
stated: Labour will address unfairness in the tax system by abolishing non-dom status and replacing it with a scheme for genuine short-term residents. They will end the use of offshore trusts for inheritance tax avoidance and close the loophole treating private equity performance-related pay as capital gains. Additionally, Labour will modernise HMRC, increasing registration and reporting requirements, strengthening powers, and investing in new technology to tackle tax avoidance by large businesses and the wealthy.

source.quote: Labour will address unfairness in the tax system. We will abolish non-dom status once and for all, replacing it with a modern scheme for people genuinely in the country for a short period. We will end the use of offshore trusts to avoid inheritance tax so that everyone who makes their home here in the UK pays their taxes here. Private equity is the only industry where performance-related pay is treated as capital gains. Labour will close this loophole. We will modernise HMRC and change the law to tackle tax avoidance. We will increase registration and reporting requirements, strengthen HMRC’s powers, invest in new technology and build capacity within HMRC. This, combined with a renewed focus on tax avoidance by large businesses and the wealthy, will begin to close the tax gap and ensure everyone pays their fair share.

bearing_set.reason: The carried-interest reform directly addresses whether performance-related pay (work income) is taxed as capital gains rather than income — a concrete pay-fairness intervention, even if it affects a narrow high-earner group.

Closes loopholes (non-dom status, PE carried interest, offshore IHT trusts) that reduce the effective tax burden on specific high-wealth individuals and PE managers — directly alters their take-home income and wealth; worsens O11 for affected groups.
Package is explicitly revenue-raising (non-dom reform, PE carry, HMRC investment); OBR/IFS have costed similar measures as improving the funded/borrowed balance, improving debt-path sustainability.

Genuinely contested mechanism: closing non-dom status and the PE carry loophole may deter high-net-worth residents and affect private equity investment in UK firms (worsening business investment indicator), but the fiscal dividend could fund productive public investment — the behavioural-response uncertainty is real and material.

Loopholes targeted (non-dom, offshore IHT trusts, PE carry) are structurally only accessible to the wealthy; closing them narrows the effective tax-rate gap between the richest and ordinary households, plausibly reducing income and wealth inequality.

membership_note: Core effects sit on fiscal sustainability (O12), inequality (O14), the tax burden on high-wealth individuals (O11), and a genuinely contested prosperity trade-off (O13). No direct effect on prices, public services, labour market quality, safety, or liberty for ordinary households that clears the non-negligible bar.
